standards.name: MiAIRR (Minimal Information about an AIRR study)
standards.abstract: MiAIRR defines metadata and minimal reporting requirements for Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire sequencing (AIRR‑seq) studies, which profile B‑cell and T‑cell receptor repertoires across subjects, samples, and sequencing experiments. The standard (developed and maintained by the AIRR Community Minimal Standards Working Group / AIRR Community) organizes metadata into six high‑level data sets (Study/Subject/Diagnosis, Sample Collection, Sample Processing & Sequencing, Raw Sequences, Data Processing, and Processed AIRR Sequences) and provides a detailed, downloadable TSV of data elements (field names, types/formats, requirement levels, definitions, and examples). MiAIRR is intended to standardize reporting to improve reproducibility, quality control, and deposition into public repositories (e.g., INSDC/SRA/BioSample) and is distributed as part of the AIRR Standards 2.0 documentation.

classification.rationale: The source provides an explicit, downloadable TSV/list-table of named metadata fields with concrete Type/Format and Level columns (i.e., a real metadata table). The material lists individual field names, data types/formats, requirement levels, definitions and examples, so the standard is best represented as a Metadata Table.

standards.name: AIRR Rearrangement Schema (V(D)J Sequences)
standards.abstract: This standard describes the representation of rearranged adaptive immune receptor sequences (e.g., antibody heavy chains or TCR beta chains) and associated annotations produced by V(D)J assignment/analysis tools. The data are recorded as tab-delimited rows (TSV) where each row is a Rearrangement object and columns correspond to specific sequence, alignment, annotation, and identifier fields. The schema is maintained by the AIRR Community and the Data Representation Working Group; it defines a recommended file format (TSV), encoding (ASCII/UTF-8), permitted data types (string, boolean, number, integer, null), boolean/null encodings, coordinate and CIGAR conventions, a set of required columns, and detailed field-level definitions to promote interoperability between tools, repositories, and analyses.

standards.name: AIRR Repertoire Schema (metadata)
standards.abstract: The AIRR Repertoire Schema describes a composite metadata object called a Repertoire that groups study, subject, sample, processing, sequencing, and rearrangement data associated with immune receptor sequencing (AIRR-seq). The recording modality is structured metadata (JSON/TSV/YAML) plus references to raw sequence files (e.g., FASTQ) and identifiers in external archives. The standard is maintained by the AIRR Community (AIRR Standards 2.0 documentation) and addresses the need to standardize metadata for AIRR-seq studies to enable programmatic access, linkage between repertoire and rearrangement objects, and consistent reporting of processing provenance. The scope covers a Repertoire object (fields such as repertoire_id, repertoire_name, repertoire_type), and references to nested objects (Study, Subject, SampleProcessing, DataProcessing) as well as detailed field-level specifications in companion tables.

standards.name: AIRR Data Schema (AIRR Standards)
standards.abstract: This standard describes metadata and data objects for Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire sequencing (AIRR-seq) studies: experimental repertoires of immune receptor sequences generated by nucleic acid sequencing (FASTQ/raw reads and processed annotated sequences). The AIRR Data Standards are versioned specifications maintained by the AIRR Community that consist of a file format and machine-readable schemas (YAML/OpenAPI). They define named schema objects (e.g., Study, Subject, Sample, Rearrangements, Repertoire) with strict typing, controlled vocabularies and ontology references to enable interoperability, programmatic validation, and data submission to AIRR Data Commons and analysis tools.

standards.name: Germline & Genotype Schema (GermlineSet, GenotypeSet)
standards.abstract: This standard describes data objects for receptor germline genes, inferred alleles, and subject genotypes for immune receptor loci (e.g., IGH, TR loci) across species. The recordings take the form of structured YAML/JSON files (or tabular TSV exports) encoding GermlineSet objects (curated lists of AlleleDescription records), supporting UnrearrangedSequence/RearrangedSequence evidence objects, and Genotype/MHCGenotype objects describing alleles found in subjects. The schema is published and maintained by the AIRR Community as part of the AIRR Standards (Germline Schema section), addressing the need for a standardised, software-consumable format to share germline gene/allele sets and genotype calls across repositories and tools. standards.name: Reactivity & Receptor Schema (AIRR Standards 2.0)
standards.abstract: This standard defines machine-readable schema objects for describing antigen reactivity measurements made on single cells (Reactivity) and the abstract representation of immunoglobulin (Ig) or T-cell receptor (TCR) molecules (Receptor). standards.name: AIRR Data Commons API (ADC API)
standards.abstract: The AIRR Data Commons API (ADC API) defines a programmatic interface for querying and retrieving processed AIRR-seq (adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing) datasets and associated metadata from a network of distributed repositories. The materials describe access to repertoire (sample-level) and rearrangement (sequence/annotation-level) objects, show concrete JSON query examples and error cases, and document design decisions and implementation guidance produced by the AIRR Common Repository Working Group. The ADC API is maintained by the AIRR Community and its Common Repository Working Group; the documents record design decisions (e.g., RESTful JSON API using OpenAPI), recommended endpoints (/repertoire and /rearrangement), query/facet behavior and response formats (JSON and TSV), and operational policies such as optional asynchronous queries and use of external discovery indexes (DataMed).

classification.rationale: The source material is primarily prose policy and design decisions (numbered decisions, meeting minutes, and narrative documentation) describing requirements, recommendations, and API features rather than a field-level metadata table or a sequential workflow. The documents present guidance and decisions (instructions/requirements) rather than a strict DAG of ordered steps or a concrete table of named fields with types.

principles.principle: Use a RESTful API, JSON, and OpenAPI specification for the ADC API.
principles.evidence:
RESTful API, JSON, using the OpenAPI specification. Initial implementation in Github

https://github.com/airr-community/airr-standards/blob/CRWG-API/specs/common_repository_api.yaml

principles.principle: Provide two primary endpoints: /repertoire and /rearrangement, representing sample repertoires and individual rearrangements respectively.
principles.evidence:
Two primary endpoints (“gettable” objects with unique ids)

/repertoire

The /repertoire endpoint returns a list of “sample repertoire objects” with associated study metadata. A sample repertoire object is the description (the metadata) of the biological sample, including the processing that is applied to that sample, that is sequenced and annotated to acquire a set of rearrangements from the sample's immune repertoire.

/rearrangement

The /rearrangement endpoint returns a list of “rearrangement objects” with associated annotations. A rearrangement object is associated with a sample repertoire by the repertoire’s unique id. A rearrangement object contains the annotation information for each sequence read, including the V, D, and J gene assignments, the Junction (CDR3 and conserved Amino Acids), as well as other relevant annotation information.

principles.principle: Adopt design ideas from the GDC API: expressive query language, field selection, loose linked data model, facets, JSON/TSV formats, and a mapping discovery endpoint.
principles.evidence:
The GDC API looks to be a good specification to build upon

https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/API/Users_Guide/Search_and_Retrieval/

* It has a well-defined and expressive query language

* Clients can limit/request what data fields to be returned (versus all data being returned)

* It has a “loose” data model, which just indicates which entities are “linked” through an endpoint and can thus be queried upon, without specifying how that link is implemented. For example, the “case” endpoint is linked to the “diagnosis” entity, so a query can be performed on diagnosis data by having “diagnosis.” as a prefix to the field name, such as “diagnosis.state”.

* It has a “facets” parameter which requests a limited form of aggregation capability, specifically for driving summary graphics (pie charts, bar plots, etc.) on a web interface.

* JSON and TSV formats for return data.

* It has a “_mapping” endpoint which is a discovery mechanism which provides metadata about the API itself. We probably need to expand upon it.

principles.principle: Specify relationships between entities in the API data model while allowing each repository to map the API to their own backend data model.
principles.evidence: We will specify relationships between entities in the API data model, but each repository can have a different backend data model, which they will need to map to the API data model.

principles.principle: Standardize response formats and flattening rules: not-flattened JSON responses; TSV for /rearrangement (not-flatten, only rearrangement data) and TSV for /repertoire as one row per repertoire with flattened study metadata.
principles.evidence:
Data for return will be:

* Not-flatten, JSON response
* TSV response for /rearrangement, not-flatten, only get rearrangement data
* TSV response for /repertoire, one row for each repertoire id, flatten all study metadata

principles.principle: Prioritize key repeating elements for precise standardization (donor species, donor health status, tissue type, cell subset, sequence type, gene usage, CDR3 sequence, receptor specificity).
principles.evidence:
Key repeating elements to prioritize for computationally precise standardization
* Donor species (e.g., homo sapiens) (subject)
* Donor health status (e.g., diabetes) (subject, primary sample)
* Tissue type (e.g. PBMC) (primary sample)
* Cell subset (e.g. T-cell)
* Sequence type (e.g., TRB) (also from primer selection - experimental protocol)
* Gene usage (e.g., IGHV1-69)
* CDR3 sequence ( e.g., “CASSYIKLN”)
* Receptor specificity (e.g., HIV virus)

principles.principle: Do not define a Registry API; use the DataMed discovery index and define a submission standard for DataMed to make AIRR repositories discoverable.
principles.evidence:
We will not define a Registry API. Instead, we will utilize the DataMed (BioCaddie) discovery index. However, CRWG will define a submission standard for DataMed so that AIRR repositories can be easily retrieved.

https://datamed.org/index.php

principles.principle: Allow multiple analytical pipelines' results to be stored; repositories should return a single default but signal alternatives and repositories decide the default.
principles.evidence:
The same raw data may be processed through multiple analytical pipelines, (e.g., for comparative purposes) with results from all pipelines in the repository. How do we indicate this and coordinate what gets returned?

Conclusion: each repository will return only one as the default, but each repository will determine its own default. CRWG API will specify the fields that get returned to alert the user that there are alternatives.

principles.principle: Do not require globally coordinated unique IDs across repositories; instead require INSDC accession numbers (BioProject, BioSample, SRA) where available to help detect duplicates.
principles.evidence:
Will we coordinate repertoire and rearrangement IDs across repositories? If yes, how?

Conclusion: it’s challenging to enforce a globally unique ID, so CRWG API will require that INSDC accession numbers (e.g., Bioproject, Biosample, SRA) are provided so users can check for duplicates. If those accession numbers aren’t available for a specific study, the user will have to rely upon manually reviewing titles, publications, abstract, etc.

principles.principle: Support asynchronous query mode as an optional capability (not required) and define its interface for repositories that choose to implement it.
principles.evidence: We will not require that repositories store the query and give it a unique identifier. However, we do see the desire for some repositories to support an asychronous query operation versus sychronous. We agreed that defining an asynchronous query mode would be useful but it places a larger burden (computational and infrastructure overhead) on the repository over a simple synchronous query mode. Therefore, we will not require repositories to support it. We will define the asynchronous query mode interface.
